title: Why I stopped chasing every framework
text:
Three years ago, I changed my main tool almost every few months. Each time a new framework appeared, I felt that I was falling behind, so I rushed to learn it, built a toy project, and moved on. My CV looked impressive. My actual skills did not.

The turning point was a job interview where I was asked to explain how a request travels from the browser to the database. I knew a dozen libraries, yet I could barely describe what happens between them. It was a humbling moment, and I still remember how my cheeks burned.

Since then I follow a simple rule. I spend most of my time on fundamentals, such as networking, data structures, and how databases store information. New tools are welcome, but only when they solve a problem I really have. Surprisingly, learning a new framework now takes a weekend, because most of its ideas are variations of things I already understand.

I do not claim that trends are worthless. They are a useful signal of where the industry is heading. But a signal is not a plan. If you are a beginner and feel overwhelmed, remember that depth beats breadth, and nobody has ever been fired for understanding HTTP too well.

questions.prompt: What problem did the author have in the past?
options: He knew many tools but understood little about how things work.
He failed because of a bad CV format.
questions.explanation: Він знав десяток бібліотек, але на співбесіді не зміг пояснити, що відбувається між ними.

questions.prompt: How does the author learn now?
options: Focuses on fundamentals and adds new tools when needed
questions.explanation: Більшість часу він витрачає на основи, а нові інструменти бере, коли вони розв'язують реальну проблему.

questions.prompt: What does the author think about trends?
options: They are the best learning plan.
They are a useful signal but not a plan.
questions.explanation: Автор називає тренди корисним сигналом, але не планом навчання.
